I am 52 years old and have farmed this same land in Quzhou for 35 years. I never went to school, but my father taught me how to read the soil and the weather, and I know my 10.1 mu better than anyone. This year will be no different from the last good years: wheat in winter, maize in summer, both on the full plot because that is how the wheat-maize system works here.

My wheat will go in this autumn with an improved variety — the same kind most of my neighbors use, because it stands well and gives steady grain. Before sowing I will run the rotary tiller to loosen the soil; wheat needs a fine seedbed. I will spread compound fertilizer as basal and then topdress with urea, about 18 kg of nitrogen per mu in total, plus phosphorus and potassium from the compound. I have a well for irrigation, so I will water three times: once after sowing if the autumn is dry, once at jointing in spring, and once at grain filling. That is what it takes to get around 500 kg per mu. I also spray four times — herbicide, insecticide, and fungicide — because if you skip even one, the rust or aphids will take your yield. My son works in the factory in town, so labor is tight, but I can handle the spraying myself and hire a machine for irrigation.

After harvesting the wheat in early June, I immediately sow maize. There is no time to plough; everyone here plants maize no-tillage straight into the wheat stubble. The stubble shades the ground and keeps moisture, which matters because June is hot. I always buy hybrid seed from the shop — never save my own, because hybrid vigor drops in the second year. Maize needs less fertilizer than wheat; I give it about 12 kg nitrogen per mu and some compound for P and K. I irrigate twice if the summer rains are thin, and I spray three times for weeds and the corn borer. If the weather is fair, I expect 550 kg per mu.

Some people say I should cut back on fertilizer to save money, but I have seen what happens when you go cheap: the ears are small and the grains are light. With my family partly working off-farm, we have a little cash to buy inputs, and I would rather spend on fertilizer and water than risk a bad year. That is how I have always done it, and that is how I will do it this year.
